title: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it's fixing that with more ads
content:
Google parent Alphabet reported its Q3 financial results on Wednesday afternoon, showing a healthy rise in revenue for the months of July to September. But the company’s stock price has taken a beating, marking one of the largest post-earnings drops in its history. It comes down to several troubling aspects of the new report, including an admission by the company that AI search isn’t earning as much as organic search, and despite that, Google expects to spend even more on AI next year.
The company took in almost $128 billion in Q3 2026, earning more than $26 billion in net income. These may sound like good numbers, but financial markets are not impressed. While revenue is up 25 percent versus last year, net income is almost $9 billion lower. As of this story’s publication, the stock price is down almost 12 percent, and it was down about 13 percent earlier in the day.
While revenue was up 25 percent year over year, analysts expected more. Google reported earnings per share of $2.12, but the consensus projection ahead of Wednesday was $3.02. Google’s Cloud products actually beat expectations, crossing $30 billion in revenue. That’s about a billion more than analyst guesses.
Google is still making a huge amount of money, but there are several troubling trends emerging. The last few years at the company have been all about AI, with generative technology appearing in products from Gmail to Android. Most notably, Google is shifting to an AI search platform powered by Gemini models.
During the earnings call, Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler discussed the company’s search volume. This is one of the key metrics by which Google tracks its own performance. In the last quarter, Google saw search grow by 12 percent versus last year. Good for the company, right? Except that’s a much slower rate than previous quarters. Growth in Q2 was 17 percent, and Q1 saw 19 percent growth over 2025. Search revenue was also flat in Q3.
So that’s the first problem, likely driven by more consumers using AI chatbots to find answers. The other issue is that Google’s take on AI search isn’t pulling in revenue like standard web search yet. According to Schindler, each AI Mode query earns less revenue compared to a similar web search—there are fewer ads, and they cost less to run.

report.summary: Google admits AI search earns less than traditional search and plans to close the gap with more ads while increasing AI spending.
report.background: Google's core search-ad business has long funded its broader ambitions, but generative AI is changing how people find information. AI chatbots and AI Overviews can answer queries directly, reducing clicks and ad slots. Google has shifted Search toward Gemini-powered AI Mode, which is popular but less monetizable than classic web search. In Q3 2026, Alphabet reported revenue up 25% to nearly $128 billion, but net income fell by almost $9 billion year over year and earnings per share missed analyst estimates. The stock dropped roughly 12-13%, reflecting investor anxiety about slowing search growth, weaker search revenue, and rising AI infrastructure costs. Cloud was a bright spot, topping $30 billion in revenue and beating expectations.
key_points: Alphabet's Q3 2026 revenue rose 25% to almost $128 billion, but net income was about $9 billion lower year over year. Earnings per share came in at $2.12 versus the $3.02 analysts expected, and the stock fell roughly 12-13%, one of Google's largest post-earnings drops.

Google's search volume growth slowed to 12% in Q3, down from 17% in Q2 and 19% in Q1. Search revenue was flat for the quarter, a worrying sign because search ads remain Google's profit engine and likely face pressure from AI chatbots.

Google confirmed that each AI Mode query generates less revenue than a comparable traditional web search. AI answers tend to show fewer ads, and those ads command lower prices, so higher AI search usage does not yet translate into proportional ad revenue.

Google says it expects to spend even more on AI next year while working to improve AI search monetization, including through more ads. That combination—slower search monetization plus rising AI capital costs—is central to investor concerns about future margins.
report.impact: The admission signals a structural shift for the AI industry: search is becoming more answer-oriented and less ad-friendly, forcing Google and rivals to redesign monetization. Expect more ads inside AI answers, sponsored citations, and commerce links, which could erode user trust if poorly executed. For developers, the pressure to build efficient retrieval, ranking, and ad-auction systems will grow, and open-source AI search alternatives may attract users wary of ad-heavy answers. For regular users, AI search may remain convenient but become more commercial, with fewer organic links and more promotional content. Google's rising AI spending also suggests infrastructure demand—chips, data centers, and energy—will stay strong, even as margins face scrutiny.
report.tools: Watch Google AI Mode and Gemini for how ads are integrated into AI answers. For hands-on exploration, try SearXNG for privacy-focused metasearch, Perplexica for AI-powered search over the web, and Open WebUI with local models for private RAG experiments. LangChain or LlamaIndex can help developers prototype retrieval and citation pipelines. Track Google Search Console changes and ad-load experiments to understand monetization shifts.
